units.title: Security goals, trust boundaries and threat models
outcomes: State confidentiality, integrity, availability and accountability (every action traceable to an identity through audit) for one service, and say which one the design trades away under pressure.
Draw assets, entry points, data flows and trust boundaries for a small RPC store.
Write abuse cases for unauthorized mutation, cross-tenant reads and restore paths, and mark each as tested or residual risk.
units.why: Every later unit assumes a written threat model. Without named assets and boundaries, least privilege and audit have nothing to attach to.

next.note: Turn the trust boundary into identities, scoped credentials and audit points.
Place residual risks into failure domains and rollout guards.

study.title: Confidentiality, integrity and availability
study.locator: Chapter 1, Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability: the Confidentiality, Integrity and Availability sections, plus Reliability Versus Security design considerations

study.title: Adversaries, profiles and methods
study.locator: Chapter 2, Understanding Adversaries: Attacker Motivations, Attacker Profiles from Hobbyists through Insiders, Attacker Methods (Threat Intelligence, Cyber Kill Chains, TTPs), Risk Assessment Considerations

study.title: System model, threat identification and mitigations
study.locator: System Modeling; Threat Identification with Choosing a Threat Modeling Technique; Response and Mitigations; Review and Validation

focus: Security controls can block recovery: in the Chapter 1 password-manager story, the safe combination sat in the offline password manager it was meant to unlock. Model recovery and on-call paths with the same care as attacks.
Adversary profiles set the budget: hobbyists through nation-states plus insiders. Defenses aim to raise attacker cost, not to stop every profile.
The system model comes first: trust boundaries, data flows, data stores, processes and external entities, then technique choice.
Each abuse case ends as a test or an explicit residual risk. Unowned risks are the failure, not the attack.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, sketch the trust-boundary diagram of a single-tenant key-value RPC service, list its assets and two adversary profiles, and write three abuse cases (unauthorized write, cross-tenant read, restore from backup), each ending in a test or a residual-risk sentence.
traps: Treating uptime as the whole goal. Redundancy that serves stale or wrong-tenant data keeps the service up while breaking integrity and confidentiality.
Modeling only external attackers. Chapter 2 treats insiders, who already hold access, as an adversary profile, and the password-manager outage needed no attacker at all.
Collecting threats without mitigations or owners. The OWASP process continues into Response and Mitigations, then Review and Validation; a list of threats is not a threat model.

selfTest.q: A service stays up during an incident but serves one tenant's records to another. Which goals failed and which held?
selfTest.a: Confidentiality and integrity failed; availability held. Uptime alone says nothing about the other two.

selfTest.q: Why does Chapter 2 advise making yourself a more expensive target even against well-funded attackers?
selfTest.a: Some attackers are economically motivated. Raising cost can remove the incentive even when perfect defense is impossible.

selfTest.q: What must the OWASP system model make clear before threat identification starts?
selfTest.a: Trust boundaries, data flows, data stores, processes and the external entities that interact with the system. These are the likely attack points that STRIDE prompts are applied to.

selfTest.q: An abuse case has no test and no owner. What is it?
selfTest.a: An unowned residual risk by default. Write it down as accepted risk or turn it into a test.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: trust-boundary diagram, abuse cases and a residual-risk statement for the RPC store and its migration path.
units.stopWhen: You can draw the boundary, name the adversaries, and close every abuse case as tested or accepted risk without reopening the books.

fit.note: The BSRS chapters and the OWASP sheet cover goals, adversaries and the modeling steps at explain depth with no gap.

units.title: Identity, authorization, least privilege and secrets
outcomes: Separate identity, authentication and authorization, and place each check in a layered service call.
Apply least privilege with small functional APIs, scoped credentials and breakglass, and state the audit cost of each exception.
Describe secret rotation and key-lifecycle vocabulary, and say where process or container isolation stops protecting secrets.
units.why: The threat model names who may cross each boundary. This unit builds the gates: identities for every caller including services, least-privilege defaults, and secrets handling that the password-manager story warns about.

next.note: Scope the identities and credentials per tenant and test the cross-tenant paths.
State where container boundaries stop protecting secrets and identities.

study.title: Least privilege, risk-ranked access and breakglass
study.locator: Chapter 5, Design for Least Privilege: Concepts and Terminology (Least Privilege, Zero Trust Networking, Zero Touch); Classifying Access Based on Risk; Best Practices (Small Functional APIs, Breakglass, Auditing); A Policy Framework for Authentication and Authorization Decisions

study.title: Identities, authentication, access control and boundaries
study.locator: Chapter 6, Design for Understandability: Understandable Identities, Authentication, and Access Control (Identities; Authentication and transport security; Access control); Security Boundaries (Small TCBs and strong security boundaries)

study.title: Authentication, access control and cryptography vocabulary
study.locator: Chapters 53 Intro Security, 54 Authentication, 55 Access Control and 56 Cryptography (the security chapter PDFs in the book table): credential, authorization-decision and key-lifecycle vocabulary
study.depth: Use for vocabulary only. Connect process and container isolation back to the threat model and state where those boundaries do not protect the system.

study.title: Secrets handling failure story
study.locator: Chapter 1, On Passwords and Power Drills: the HSM smart-card restart failure and the safe combination stored in the offline password manager

focus: Identity covers services and hardware, not only humans: the snapshot and quota call chain in Chapter 6 needs a credential at every hop.
Small functional APIs are the auditing advantage: breakglass sessions and direct credential handouts cannot produce granular trails.
Credentials assert identity through a protocol (password, X.509 certificate, OAuth2 token). Authorization is a separate policy decision.
Rotation is measured work: Chapter 8 advises measuring key rotation cycles, and Chapter 9 covers rotating signing keys under rollback.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write the authentication and authorization policy for a two-service chain (frontend calls backend calls store): name each identity, credential type and check, scope one credential to a single operation, and describe the breakglass path plus what its audit record can and cannot show.
traps: Storing the recovery secret inside the system it recovers. The safe combination lived in the offline password manager.
Treating authentication as authorization. A valid credential identifies the caller; the policy still decides the operation.
Assuming containers add access control. Namespaces and cgroups isolate processes and resources; they do not authenticate callers or scope credentials.

selfTest.q: A service presents a valid token for a snapshot operation it was never granted. Which check failed?
selfTest.a: Authorization. Authentication succeeded; the policy decision for that operation is a separate step.

selfTest.q: Why do small functional APIs improve auditing more than any log format?
selfTest.a: Each call is one granular action with its parameters, so the log states exactly what happened. A broad interactive session log cannot.

selfTest.q: An on-call engineer uses breakglass during an outage. What must happen after?
selfTest.a: The exceptional access is audited and reviewed, and the temporary grant expires or is revoked. Breakglass is exceptional by design.

selfTest.q: Where do container boundaries stop helping with secrets?
selfTest.a: At identity and access: a secret mounted into the container is visible to every process that can read it. Scoping and rotation still apply inside.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: authenticated service boundaries, scoped credentials with expiry, and audit tests that reject over-scoped and expired credentials.
units.stopWhen: You can place every identity, credential, policy check and audit point on the call chain and defend the breakglass scope from memory.

fit.note: Least privilege, identities and secrets are covered at explain depth by the BSRS chapters and OSTEP vocabulary with no gap.

units.title: Tenant isolation, input validation and injection
outcomes: Scope every data path by tenant identity and reject cross-tenant reads through normal, retry and cache paths.
Replace string-built queries with parameterized queries and type-level SQL boundaries, and validate inputs with allowlists.
Refuse native deserialization of untrusted bytes and use pure-data formats with signed envelopes where needed.
units.why: Assumes the Programming units on relational SQL queries and idempotent HTTP APIs as background. This unit takes their endpoint into the storage engine and the wire format, where one missing tenant predicate or one pickle load leaks or corrupts another tenant's data.

next.note: Log tenant-scoped decisions with redacted telemetry.
Keep tenant identifiers low-cardinality and secret-free in metrics and traces.

study.title: Framework enforcement, SQL injection and XSS types
study.locator: Chapter 12, Writing Code: Frameworks to Enforce Security and Reliability (Example Framework for RPC Backends); SQL Injection Vulnerabilities: `TrustedSqlString`, from the password-reset concatenation example through bound parameters and prepared statements; Preventing XSS: `SafeHtml`

study.title: Security boundaries, blast radius and data isolation
study.locator: Chapter 8, Design for Resilience: Controlling the Blast Radius (Role Separation, Location Separation with Isolation of trust and Isolation of confidentiality); Failure Domains and Redundancies (Failure Domains with Data isolation)

study.title: Allowlist validation and parsing discipline
study.locator: Input Validation Strategies (Allowlist vs Denylist); Implementing Input Validation (Parse Safely, Then Validate; Validate Structured Data); Common Pitfalls (client-only checks, trusting internal sources, denylisting, logging rejected input verbatim)

study.title: Safe deserialization rules
study.locator: Python Clear-box Review (`pickle.load` and `pickle.loads`, unsafe PyYAML loaders, `jsonpickle.decode`); Language-Agnostic Methods (Using Alternative Data Formats, Only Deserialize Signed Data)

focus: Tenant identity is an authorization input, not a request field: the query predicate comes from the authenticated context, never from the body.
Parameterization plus type boundaries: bound parameters separate code from data, and `TrustedSqlString`-style types make mixing impossible by construction.
Validate the representation that is used: decode once per protocol, then allowlist syntax and semantics. Denylists and client-only checks do not hold.
Native formats execute: `pickle`, unsafe YAML and type-driven JSON decoders run code at load time, so untrusted bytes get pure-data formats only.
units.reproduce: In a scratch SQLite database with two tenants, run a tenant filter built by string interpolation with the value `acme' OR '1'='1` and show it returns both tenants' rows; then run the parameterized tenant-scoped query and show it returns only the caller tenant's single row. Then show `pickle.loads` executing a planted reduce call while `json.loads` of the same fields returns plain data.
traps: Adding tenant checks on the main path but not on retry, cache-fill or restore paths. Every path that reads or writes tenant data needs the predicate and a test.
Checking a deserialized object after loading it. Execution can happen during load, so the type test comes too late.
Validating before the final decode. A downstream decode can change meaning after the check passed.

selfTest.q: The tenant id arrives both in the auth token and the JSON body, and they disagree. Which one scopes the query?
selfTest.a: The auth token. The body is untrusted input; the predicate uses the authenticated context.

selfTest.q: Why is a guideline to use prepared statements weaker than a `TrustedSqlString`-style type?
selfTest.a: Guidelines need every developer and reviewer to comply every time. The type makes untrusted SQL construction impossible by construction.

selfTest.q: A cache fills a missed entry with another tenant's row and serves it on retry. Which boundary failed?
selfTest.a: Tenant isolation on the cache-fill path. Every data path carries the tenant predicate, not only the primary query.

selfTest.q: Untrusted YAML arrives. Which loader, and why?
selfTest.a: A safe loader that builds only plain data and blocks custom constructors, because unsafe loaders instantiate arbitrary objects.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: tenant-scoped queries across normal, retry, cache and restore paths, plus injection and deserialization tests with fixed fixtures.
units.stopWhen: Your scratch demo shows the bypass and the fix, and you can name every path where the tenant predicate must appear.

fit.note: Coverage failed for input-validation and deserialization depth; the OWASP Input Validation and Deserialization sheets fill those beside the BSRS chapters.

units.title: Audit records, fail-open versus fail-closed and supply chain
outcomes: Write audit records that state who did what with which parameters, and redact secrets before they reach telemetry.
Choose fail-closed versus fail-open per operation, and defend the default when policy or time data is missing.
Name the supply-chain control points from code review to provenance-checked deployment, and the adversary each one stops.
units.why: Assumes the Programming unit on logs, metrics and traces (bounded labels, secret exclusion, OpenTelemetry) as background. This unit adds the audit contract around it: tamper-evident records, explicit failure defaults, and build-to-deploy provenance.

next.note: Carry audit and revocation behavior through rollback and migration.
Feed audit trails into incident timelines and postmortems.

study.title: Collecting auditable records
study.locator: Chapter 5, Best Practices: Auditing (Collecting good audit logs, Choosing an auditor); Graceful Failure and Breakglass Mechanisms

study.title: Failing safe versus failing secure
study.locator: Chapter 8, Automate Responsibly: Failing safe versus failing secure (allow-all versus deny-all default ACLs when integrity is unverified)

study.title: Revocation, failing open and intended state
study.locator: Chapter 9, Design Principles for Recovery: Use an Explicit Revocation Mechanism (centralized revocation service, Failing open with the time-service outage example, Revoking credentials at scale); Know Your Intended State, Down to the Bytes

study.title: Supply-chain threat model and provenance
study.locator: Chapter 14, Deploying Code: Threat Model (benign insiders, malicious insiders, compromised accounts); Best Practices (Require Code Reviews, Verify Artifacts, Not Just People); Advanced Mitigation Strategies (Binary Provenance, Provenance-Based Deployment Policies); Deployment Choke Points
study.depth: Read for control points and vocabulary, not build-system implementation.

focus: Audit the useful parameters: small APIs make each record one granular action, while broad sessions cannot be audited meaningfully.
Failing open trades lockout risk for attacker reuse: a revocation service that accepts stale credentials during a time-service outage revalidates revoked keys.
Prefer cached revocation data with best-known state over timeout-and-allow. State which clock or freshness assumption each choice keeps.
Verify artifacts, not people: reviews, tests, provenance and deployment choke points each stop a different supply-chain adversary.
units.reproduce: Build a three-event hash-chained audit log in scratch code: show a redaction rule keeping a login token out of the chain, tamper with one record and show verification failing, and show an authorize stub denying when the policy is unloaded and allowing the same call when it is loaded.
traps: Logging secrets to make audit complete. Completeness never justifies credentials in logs; record the key id and the decision instead.

Assuming fail-open is the reliable choice everywhere. Chapter 8 says security-critical operations should not fail open, because a denial of service alone would then weaken security; revocation keeps last-known-good data instead.
Trusting build-time checks while deployments bypass them. Controls must reject artifacts that skip the chain.

selfTest.q: The certificate validity database cannot reach the time service. Why is accept-on-timeout dangerous?
selfTest.a: Revoked certificates read as valid for the whole outage, and a cheap DoS on the time service extends it. Cache revocation data instead.

selfTest.q: What must an audit record of a grant contain, and what must it never contain?
selfTest.a: Actor, action, scope and parameters such as key id; never the secret itself.

selfTest.q: A binary reaches production without passing CI. Which control failed?
selfTest.a: The deployment choke point. Build checks cannot help if deployment accepts unprovenanced artifacts.

selfTest.q: ACLs fail to load. What default does a reliability-first design assume, what does a security-first design assume, and which wins for a security-critical operation?
selfTest.a: Allow all versus deny all. Security-critical operations should not fail open; they may degrade to a lower-cost component that applies stronger controls, not weaker ones.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: audit tests for unauthorized and cross-tenant attempts, plus backup and restore verification with integrity checks.
units.stopWhen: You can defend the fail-open versus fail-closed default of each gate and trace one artifact from review to provenanced deployment.

fit.note: Auditing, failure defaults, revocation and supply-chain controls are covered at explain depth by the BSRS chapters with no gap.

units.title: Membership inference, extraction, inversion and poisoning
outcomes: Threat-model membership inference, extraction, inversion and poisoning for one model endpoint, and separate privacy loss from integrity loss.
Run a loss-threshold membership attack with a non-overfit control and report AUC with sample sizes.
Describe backdoor poisoning under a weak threat model and state the serving-side exfiltration path it opens.
units.why: Models exposed as endpoints leak through their outputs. This unit measures how much, with a control, before the next unit spends a privacy budget to stop it.

next.note: Spend a measured budget against the attacks quantified here.

study.depth: Read as aggregate-query attacks that motivate noise, not as model attacks. The model attacks are the lecture's sections above.

study.title: Privacy-attack taxonomy and threat model
study.locator: Attack taxonomy and threat model (adversarial knowledge, assets under attack); causes of privacy leaks; defenses overview and open problems
study.depth: Survey, not a textbook: read the taxonomy and one attack family end to end, and skip the per-paper catalog.

study.title: Backdoor poisoning result
study.locator: Threat model (no model or training-set knowledge, small poisoning fraction, stealthy key) and evaluation (about 50 poisoning samples, above 90 percent attack success)
study.depth: Read the threat model and results; skip the optimization details. Defensive and conceptual only: study the poisoning pattern, never deploy a backdoor.

focus: Fix goal, access and knowledge first: the image-API and hospital examples change what black-box versus white-box even means.
Cheap metrics beat shadow models for the demo: correctness, loss, confidence and entropy all read the same overfitting gap.
Extraction is sampling plus membership ranking: perplexity selects the memorized sequences out of many samples.
Empirical defenses are claims until attacked: Kerckhoffs-style evaluation tries to break the defense before trusting it.
units.reproduce: With CPython 3.14.4, scikit-learn 1.9.1 and NumPy 2.5.4, draw 500 points from a 20-dimensional standard normal with uniform random 0/1 labels (`default_rng(0)`); the first 60 are members, the other 440 nonmembers. Fit a `StandardScaler` on the members, then train an unregularized MLP (hidden layers 128 and 64, `alpha` 0, `max_iter` 5000, `random_state` 0) and a `LogisticRegression` control with `C=1e-4`. Score each point by minus its loss on the true label (probability clipped at `1e-15`). The memorizer gives AUC 0.865 (train accuracy 1.000, mean member loss 0.003, nonmember 2.185); the control gives 0.584 (train accuracy 0.533). Across seeds 0 to 4 the ranges are 0.865 to 0.948 and 0.556 to 0.602.
traps: Reporting attack AUC without the control. Even the near-chance control scores 0.556 to 0.602, so the gap, not the level, is the evidence.

Reading the lecture's correctness-attack intuition as written. Its text swaps train and test: the model classifies most of its training data correctly and a smaller fraction of unseen data, and the attack exploits that gap.
Treating a weakened attack demo as protection. Regularization and output rounding only narrow the gap until a stronger attack is tried.

selfTest.q: What does a loss-threshold attack output, and how is the threshold picked?
selfTest.a: Member when the point loss is below \(\tau\). \(\tau\) can come from published train-loss statistics; the demo avoids picking one by reporting threshold-free AUC.

selfTest.q: Why does extraction rank samples by perplexity?
selfTest.a: Memorized sequences get high predicted probability token by token, hence low perplexity. Sampling proposes candidates; ranking selects likely members.

selfTest.q: A defense drops the attack AUC from 0.9 to 0.6. Is the leak fixed?
selfTest.a: Not shown. A new attack or more queries can reopen it; only a budgeted guarantee bounds all attacks in the threat model.

selfTest.q: How do poisoning and inversion differ in what they break?
selfTest.a: Poisoning breaks integrity by planting behavior through training data; inversion breaks privacy by recovering inputs through outputs.

practice.name: MIT Data-Centric AI: Lab - Membership Inference notebook

units.stopWhen: You can run the attack with its control, quote both AUCs with sample sizes, and threat-model one endpoint across all four attack families.

units.title: Differential privacy: adjacency, sensitivity, noise and composition
outcomes: Define adjacency, unit of privacy, sensitivity and the \((\epsilon, \delta)\) guarantee for one aggregate.
Build a clamped Laplace release, derive its \(\epsilon\) from sensitivity over scale, and compose two releases.
Measure utility loss against the true aggregate and list every component outside the guarantee.
units.why: The only privacy claim in this stage with a proof. Everything outside the stated mechanism, adjacency and budget keeps no promise.

next.note: Version the bounds, budget and accounting inputs so migration cannot silently change them.

study.title: Adjacency, sensitivity and privacy maps
study.locator: A Framework to Understand DP: Distance Between Datasets - Adjacency (symmetric distance); Definition of Privacy; Distance Between Aggregates - Sensitivity (clamped sum); Stability Maps and Privacy Maps (chained Laplace sum with \(\epsilon\) 0.48)

study.title: Clamp, sum and Laplace chaining in code
study.locator: Differential Privacy with OpenDP: The Laplace Mechanism; Transformation Example: Sum; Transformation Example: Clamp; Chaining (clamp, bounded sum and Laplace composed with the privacy map); Retrospective
study.depth: Run the examples with OpenDP 0.16.0, the version these pages document. `make_sequential_composition` groups releases under one budget.

study.title: Accuracy limits of noisy releases
study.locator: Accuracy: Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Accuracy vs Confidence Intervals; What is \(D\) (preprocessing and resize effects on the guarantee target)

study.title: The \((\epsilon, \delta)\) definition and DP-SGD
study.locator: Towards a solution: differential privacy (the \((\epsilon, \delta)\) inequality over adjacent datasets; DP-SGD as the training analogue; parameter-setting and utility challenges)

focus: Adjacency is the whole promise: symmetric distance 1 means adding or removing one record, and multi-row contributors scale the bound by \(k\).
Clamping sets sensitivity before noise means anything: with bounds `(0, 10)` one record moves the sum by at most 10, so Laplace scale 10 buys \(\epsilon\) about 1.
Chaining multiplies the reasoning: the clamp map fed into the noise map gives the release map, and sequential composition adds epsilons across releases.
Accuracy utilities bound noise error only: the guarantee covers the release minus the true aggregate, never the sample minus the population.
units.reproduce: With OpenDP 0.16.0 (contrib enabled) on CPython 3.14.4, chain clamp to `(0, 10)`, sum and Laplace scale 10 over float vectors under symmetric distance. `map(1)` returns `1.000000009313226`: the sum reports sensitivity `10.00000009313226` to cover float rounding, and the Laplace map alone turns 10 into exactly 1.0. Draw 200 values uniform on `[0, 10]` with NumPy `default_rng(7)` (true clamped sum 1005.9) and make 2000 releases. OpenDP draws noise from its own unseeded generator, so the mean absolute error changes per run: three runs gave 9.79, 9.96 and 10.03 against the Laplace mean absolute deviation of 10 (standard error about 0.22). Then derive that two such releases compose to \(\epsilon\) about 2.0.
traps: Quoting \(\epsilon\) without adjacency, bounds and \(\delta\). The number is meaningless until the unit of privacy and the clamp are stated.
Reading accuracy output as a confidence interval for the population. It covers noise around this dataset aggregate only.
Assuming the guarantee covers the pipeline. Ingestion, bounds choice, budget accounting and the served model sit outside unless each is modeled.

selfTest.q: Bounds are `(0, 10)` and one person contributes one row. What is the clamped-sum sensitivity?
selfTest.a: 10. Removing or adding one clamped record changes the sum by at most the clamp range.

selfTest.q: Scale is 10 and sensitivity is 10. What \(\epsilon\), and what changes with scale 5?
selfTest.a: About 1.0. Scale 5 doubles it to about 2.0 and halves the noise: \(\epsilon\) equals sensitivity divided by scale.

selfTest.q: Two \(\epsilon\)-1.0 releases run on the same data. What is the pair budget?
selfTest.a: About 2.0 by basic sequential composition. Each release spends separately against the same adjacency.

selfTest.q: \(\delta\) is 0 for this Laplace release. What does \(\delta\) allow in general?
selfTest.a: An additive slack in the guarantee, informally a small probability that the \(\epsilon\) bound does not hold, as with the Gaussian mechanism. Pure Laplace keeps \(\delta\) at 0.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: one clipped and noised aggregate with stated adjacency, \(\epsilon\) and \(\delta\) inputs, measured utility and a residual-risk statement.
units.stopWhen: You can derive \(\epsilon\) from bounds and scale, quote measured error with its setup, and name everything the guarantee excludes.

fit.note: The OpenDP theory notebooks cover adjacency through accounting and the lecture adds the \((\epsilon, \delta)\) definition; composition is derived in the card from that definition.

units.title: Compatibility, rollback and revocation during changes
outcomes: State compatibility rules for schema and protocol changes, and gate rollout on explicit version signals.
Plan canary, rollback and backup-restore so a bad release or a revoked credential cannot strand the system.
Carry tenant isolation, audit and privacy accounting across migration and restore paths.
units.why: Assumes the Programming units on schema migrations with Alembic and idempotency-key ledgers as background. This unit adds the failure-aware half: rollback that does not revive vulnerabilities, revocation that works during outages, and restores that keep tenant boundaries.

next.note: Apply canary and rollback mechanics to the migration plan.
Turn the migration runbook into an incident timeline when it fails.

study.locator: Chapter 7, Design for a Changing Landscape: Types of Security Changes; Architecture Decisions to Make Changes Easier (Keep Dependencies Up to Date, Release Frequently); Different Changes: Short-Term Change (Shellshock), Medium-Term Change (FIDO keys), Long-Term Change (HTTPS)

study.title: Rollback trade-offs and revocation
study.locator: Chapter 9, Design Principles for Recovery: Rollbacks Represent a Tradeoff (Deny lists, Minimum Acceptable Security Version Numbers, Rotating signing keys); Use an Explicit Revocation Mechanism (Handling emergencies directly, Revoking credentials at scale); Know Your Intended State, Down to the Bytes

study.title: Deployment policy and breakglass
study.locator: Chapter 14, Deploying Code: Provenance-Based Deployment Policies (Implementing policy decisions); Post-Deployment Verification; Practical Advice (Take It One Step at a Time, Include a Deployment Breakglass)

focus: Different changes move at different speeds: zero-days, posture improvements and external demands each get their own timeline and test budget.
Rollback trades reliability against security: minimum version numbers, deny lists and key rotation stop a rollback from reviving holes.
Revocation must work while hurt: cached revocation lists beat fail-open timeouts, and emergencies go through the same list mechanism, not hand-edited key files or a rarely used emergency list.
Know the intended bytes: host, firmware and data state are declared before migration so verification has something to compare.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write the migration plan for a versioned RPC store: a compatibility table for one schema change, canary and rollback triggers, a revocation step that works with the time service down, and a restore check that re-verifies tenant predicates and the DP accounting inputs.
traps: Rolling back to a version with a known hole to fix an outage. Minimum acceptable versions exist for exactly this moment.
Depending on accurate time during revocation. Clocks are an external dependency; cached revocation data removes it.
Migrating privacy bounds or budgets silently. Bounds, \(\epsilon\) and \(\delta\) inputs and the spent budget are versioned configuration and state, not code constants.

selfTest.q: A rollback fixes availability but revives a patched injection. What control should have stopped it?
selfTest.a: A minimum acceptable security version number. Rollback targets below it are refused even in an outage.

selfTest.q: Why does the book prefer cached revocation lists over fail-open on timeout?
selfTest.a: Cached lists keep the best-known deny state without a live dependency. Fail-open revalidates revoked credentials for the whole outage.

selfTest.q: What does a canary buy that a fast full rollout does not?
selfTest.a: A bounded blast radius: production signals from a small slice before full exposure. A fast rollout can be right for an actively exploited zero-day, but it gives up that check.

selfTest.q: A restore brings back last month's tenant table. What must the restore check?
selfTest.a: Tenant predicates, credential validity and accounting inputs against current versions. Restored data must not widen access or budgets.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: canary and rollback drill, backup-restore verification, and a revocation check under a failed dependency.
units.stopWhen: You can walk a schema change from canary through rollback or revoke without dropping isolation, audit or budget accounting.

fit.note: Change management, rollback, revocation and deployment controls are covered at explain depth by the BSRS chapters with no gap.
